## Why this unit matters

- Every earlier chapter built a **process model**: rules that generate the latent
  epidemic trajectory.
- Surveillance data are never the latent process — they are **noisy, partial
  counts**.
- An **observation model** links the two, and is what you must state before
  anyone can fit anything.

**Noise moves house.** This morning it was in the process, where events fired
at random. Here the process goes back to being a deterministic ODE and *all* the
randomness sits in the measurement.

::: {.notes}
Deal with the switch head-on, because it looks like a step backwards after two
sessions arguing that process noise changes the answer. Two separate questions:
does the epidemic itself unfold randomly, and is what we observe a noisy view of
it? This morning answered the first and held the second fixed; this session does
the reverse, which isolates one thing at a time. Real analyses need both layers,
and the reason to hold the process deterministic here is that it makes the
observation layer's effect unmistakable rather than tangled up with fade-out.

Keep the process/observation split explicit throughout. Chapters 8 and 9 estimate
process parameters *through* this observation layer, so the modelling choices made
here propagate directly into any inference results. Note that those are
self-study chapters, not workshop sessions.
:::

## Process and observation, side by side

Baseline SIR with a cumulative-incidence state $C$
($S_0=990, I_0=10, R_0=0, N=1000, c=10, \beta=0.05, \gamma=0.25$):

$$
\dot S=-\beta c\tfrac{SI}{N},\quad
\dot I=\beta c\tfrac{SI}{N}-\gamma I,\quad
\dot R=\gamma I,\quad
\dot C=\beta c\tfrac{SI}{N}.
$$

| | Process | Observation |
|---|---|---|
| Determinism | deterministic | stochastic |
| Time | continuous | discrete (daily) |
| State | continuous counts $S,I,R,C$ | integer counts $Y_t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ |

::: {.notes}
Only *new* infections generate reports, so the signal is incidence, not
prevalence. The latent daily incidence is the increment of $C$.
:::

## Count models: Poisson vs negative-binomial

Latent incidence $x_t=C(t)-C(t-1)$; reporting fraction $\rho$:

$$
Y_t\mid x_t\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\rho x_t),\qquad
\mathbb E[Y_t]=\operatorname{Var}[Y_t]=\rho x_t,
$$

$$
Y_t\mid x_t\sim\operatorname{NegBin}\!\Big(r,\tfrac{r}{r+\rho x_t}\Big),\quad
\operatorname{Var}[Y_t]=\rho x_t+\tfrac{(\rho x_t)^2}{r}.
$$

Poisson is **equidispersed**; the negative-binomial adds overdispersion and
recovers Poisson as $r\to\infty$.

::: {.notes}
Real surveillance is almost always overdispersed, and the dispersion $r$ is the
one extra parameter that buys a defensible variance. Be precise about what it
does: it widens each day's marginal distribution and nothing more. Batching and
weekday effects correlate neighbouring days, which a per-day variance cannot
represent, and super-spreading is variation in transmission — process noise, not
reporting noise.
:::

## Simulating case reports

```{julia}
#| label: fig-slide-ch07-obs
#| fig-cap: "Latent daily incidence (line) with one Poisson (left) and one overdispersed negative-binomial (right) realisation. Same latent mean, wider negative-binomial scatter."
using CairoMakie
using EpiModelingCourse
using OrdinaryDiffEq
using Distributions
using StableRNGs
CairoMakie.activate!(type = "png")

# The process kernel and baseline come from the course package, so the deck,
# the book chapter and the notebook run the same code.
p07 = BASELINE_PARAMETERS
prob07 = ODEProblem(sir_cumulative_ode!, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0, 0.0], (0.0, 40.0), p07)
sol07 = solve(prob07, Tsit5(); saveat = 1.0, abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10)
obstimes07 = 1.0:1.0:40.0
cum07 = Array(sol07)[4, :]
incidence07 = cum07[2:end] .- cum07[1:(end - 1)]

pois07 = rand.(StableRNG(20240607), Poisson.(incidence07))
r07 = 10.0
nb07(μ) = NegativeBinomial(r07, r07 / (r07 + μ))
rng07 = StableRNG(20240608)
negbin07 = [rand(rng07, nb07(μ)) for μ in incidence07]

fig07 = Figure(size = (900, 360))
for (col, obs, ttl) in ((1, pois07, "Poisson"),
                        (2, negbin07, "Negative-binomial (r=10)"))
    ax = Axis(fig07[1, col]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "new cases/day",
        title = ttl)
    barplot!(ax, collect(obstimes07), obs; color = (:darkorange, 0.5))
    lines!(ax, collect(obstimes07), incidence07; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3)
end
fig07
```

::: {.notes}
Each observation model gets its own `StableRNG` so the streams are independent
and reproducible. The full book chapter also derives incidence with a
`PresetTimeCallback` reset and a delay differential equation, and prefers plain
differencing for downstream inference.
:::

## Validation and dispersion

```{julia}
#| label: ch07-validation
S07 = Array(sol07)[1, :]
conservation = maximum(abs.(cum07 .- (990.0 .- S07)))
# Replicate-based dispersion at the epidemic peak (fixed latent mean).
peak = argmax(incidence07)
pois_rep = [rand(StableRNG(s), Poisson(incidence07[peak])) for s in 1:2000]
nb_rep = [rand(StableRNG(s), nb07(incidence07[peak])) for s in 1:2000]
(conservation_error = round(conservation; sigdigits = 2),
 poisson_var_over_mean = round(var(pois_rep) / mean(pois_rep); digits = 2),
 negbin_var_over_mean = round(var(nb_rep) / mean(nb_rep); digits = 2))
```

- **Conservation:** $C(t)=S_0-S(t)$ to solver tolerance.
- At the peak, **replicate** Poisson counts are equidispersed
  ($\text{var}/\text{mean}\approx1$); negative-binomial counts are overdispersed.

::: {.notes}
Dispersion must be measured across *replicates at a fixed time*, not along the
time series, whose spread reflects the epidemic curve. Averaging thousands of
Poisson realisations back to the latent mean is the book chapter's third check.
:::

## Julia API

```julia
using EpiModelingCourse   # sir_cumulative_ode!, synthetic_incidence
df = synthetic_incidence(; seed = 1, tspan = (0.0, 40.0),
                         observation_noise = :poisson, reporting_rate = 1.0)

using Distributions       # Poisson, NegativeBinomial
using StableRNGs          # StableRNG(seed) for reproducible streams
```

- `OrdinaryDiffEq` integrates the cumulative-incidence ODE.
- `Distributions` supplies the count models; `StableRNG` fixes the seed.

::: {.notes}
The course package `synthetic_incidence` returns a stable-schema `DataFrame`
(`time, S, I, R, cumulative_incidence, incidence, expected_incidence,
observed_incidence`) so the chapter, slides and notebook share one generator.
:::

## Takeaways and limitations

- Separate the **latent process** from the **observation process**.
- Poisson understates uncertainty when reporting is clustered; use the
  negative-binomial.
- $\rho$ rescales the expected counts; $\beta$ also changes growth rate and peak
  timing — strongly correlated, **not interchangeable**. The next session names this.
- We assumed instantaneous, conditionally independent reporting — real systems
  add delays and weekday effects.

Read the [book chapter](../../chapters/09-observation-models.html); see
[Distributions.jl](https://juliastats.org/Distributions.jl/stable/) and
[StableRNGs.jl](https://github.com/JuliaRandom/StableRNGs.jl).

::: {.notes}
Be careful with the reporting-fraction bullet: it is a statement about how hard
the two are to separate, not a claim that it is impossible. Halving rho and
doubling beta does not give the same epidemic, because it shifts the peak day,
so the curve does carry the information in principle. What is true is that the two are
strongly correlated, and the last session shows exactly what has to be known
about the population before they come apart at all.

Close by pointing at the two inference chapters, the frequentist parameter estimation chapter by maximum
likelihood and the Bayesian inference chapter by Bayesian sampling, while saying clearly that they are
self-study, not sessions here, and that the programme page names the LSHTM course
for anyone who wants to go further with fitting.
:::
